blocks.content: Chandigarh punches well above its tiny geographic weight economically — it consistently ranks among India's highest per-capita-income states/UTs, a headline statistic that shows up constantly in comparative economy questions across exams.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The economy is fundamentally organized into primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors.
Industrial performance depends on manufacturing, core infrastructure, and energy output.
Trade and retail sectors play a crucial role in economic distribution and consumer access.
Ease of living metrics measure regulatory efficiency, service access, and overall quality of life.

blocks.content: Chandigarh's economy is overwhelmingly services-led — driven by public administration/government employment (as capital of two states plus its own UT administration), education, healthcare, IT/ITeS, retail, and tourism — with almost no agriculture given the UT's tiny, largely urbanised land area.

The city has consistently ranked among the top Indian states/UTs by per-capita income, a fact regularly used in comparative economic-geography questions (commonly cited alongside Delhi, Goa, and Sikkim as high-per-capita performers).

Chandigarh IT Park (Rajiv Gandhi Chandigarh Technology Park) in the city's southern sectors hosts IT/ITeS companies and has been positioned as the anchor of the UT's technology-sector growth, though on a much smaller scale than metros like Bengaluru or Gurugram.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: 'Tricity' = Chandigarh + Panchkula (Haryana) + Mohali/SAS Nagar (Punjab) — a functionally integrated urban economic region straddling all three jurisdictions, frequently referenced in both economy and urban-geography questions.

items: The Industrial Area (Phase I and Phase II) hosts small and medium enterprises focused on auto parts, machine tools, electronics assembly, and light engineering goods, deliberately zoned away from residential sectors under Le Corbusier's original 'Hand' (industrial) designation in his body metaphor for the city.

Larger heavy industry is discouraged within the UT itself by policy and available land constraints, with heavier manufacturing instead clustering in neighbouring Punjab and Haryana industrial towns (e.g., Mohali, Derabassi, Panchkula, Baddi across the Himachal border).

Chandigarh has positioned itself as a hub for education-linked and health-linked service industries — private hospitals, coaching institutes, and higher-education campuses draw a large catchment population from Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh.
Classification of primary, secondary, and tertiary economic activities is frequently tested.
Indices related to Industrial Production (IIP) and core sector output are key exam topics.
Parameters defining Ease of Doing Business and Ease of Living are high-yield areas for competitive exams.
Sector 17 functions as the city's central business district and main commercial/shopping hub — Le Corbusier's designated 'heart' of the city.

Chandigarh has repeatedly ranked highly in national Ease of Living Index and cleanliness/liveability surveys among smaller cities and UTs, reflecting its planned infrastructure, high literacy, and civic service levels.

The UT has one of India's highest rates of vehicle ownership per capita, a byproduct of its planned wide roads, high per-capita income, and relatively low population density compared to unplanned Indian cities of similar population.
Chandigarh's economy is services-dominated; agriculture is negligible given its almost fully urbanised land.
Consistently ranks among India's top states/UTs by per-capita income.
'Tricity' = Chandigarh + Panchkula (Haryana) + Mohali/SAS Nagar (Punjab) — an integrated cross-state urban economic region.
Rajiv Gandhi Chandigarh Technology Park is the UT's key IT/ITeS hub.
Sector 17 = the city's central business district, Le Corbusier's designated 'heart' of Chandigarh.
Chandigarh ranks among the highest in India for per-capita vehicle ownership and liveability/cleanliness indices.
